extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of elementary number theory and introductory algebra/analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapters giving statements and proofs of classical results: representation of integers as sums of two squares, Wedderburn's theorem on finite division rings, irrationality results (e, pi-related), and Euler's zeta(2)=pi^2/6 with several proofs. Focus is on elementary proofs and techniques (modular arithmetic, pigeonhole, involutions, cyclotomic polynomials, integral transforms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1: characterization of -1 as square mod p
rubrics_metrics.description: For primes p = 4m + 1 the equation s^2 = -1 (mod p) has two solutions s in {1,2,...,p-1}; for p = 2 there is one solution; for primes p = 4m + 3 there is no solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs an equivalence relation on {1,...,p-1} identifying x with -x and with multiplicative inverse; equivalence classes are typically quadruples, except possibly pairs {1,p-1} and a second pair when p-1 is multiple of 4, which yields the two solutions. Examples: p=11 and p=13 partitions illustrated; use this lemma to find s with s^2 = -1 (mod p) when p≡1 (mod4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2: no 4m+3 number is sum of two squares
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural number n ≡ 3 (mod 4) can be represented as a sum of two integer squares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason: squares mod 4 are 0 or 1, so sums of two squares are 0,1,2 (mod 4), never 3. Use to identify 'bad' primes of form 4m+3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition: primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) are sum of two squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Every prime of the form p = 4m + 1 can be written p = x^2 + y^2 for some natural numbers x,y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proofs given. (1) Thue/pigeonhole-style proof: use many pairs (x',y') in range and pigeonhole modulo p to produce nonzero (x,y) with x^2 + y^2 = p. (2) Heath-Brown involution (Book Proof): study integer solutions of 4xy+z^2=p and apply three linear involutions (interchange x,y and negate z; a hidden involution g; trivial involution) to deduce existence of solution with x=y leading to representation. Notes: both proofs are non-effective for large primes; references for efficient algorithms are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime fields: basic properties used in modular arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If p is prime then Z_p = {0,1,...,p-1} is a finite field; for x≠0 additive inverse is p-x, multiplicative inverse exists and the map z↦xz is a permutation on Z_p\{0}; squares 0^2,1^2,...,h^2 (with h=floor(p/2)) produce (h+1) distinct squares in Z_p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly for counting arguments: e.g., counting squares and numbers of the form -(1+y^2) guarantees solutions to x^2 + y^2 ≡ -1 (mod p) by pigeonhole-type cardinality. Useful reminders: injectivity→surjectivity on finite sets; behavior of inverses; parity observations (x and -x distinct if p>2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization theorem: which n are sums of two squares
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural number n can be represented as a sum of two squares iff every prime factor p ≡ 3 (mod 4) appears with an even exponent in the prime factorization of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to five facts: (1) small base representables (1,2) and primes p≡1 (mod4) are representable; (2) product of representables is representable by identity n1 n2 = (x1 x2 + y1 y2)^2 + (x1 y2 - x2 y1)^2; (3) multiplying a representable number by a square preserves representability; (4) if p≡3 (mod4) divides representable n=x^2+y^2 then p divides both x and y, hence p^2|n; (5) iteration yields that p^2 divides n and quotient is representable. These items together give 'if and only if'. Guidance includes how to combine multiplicativity and local divisibility constraints; corollary: infinitely many primes p≡1 (mod4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid-style infinitude arguments for primes in arithmetic progressions (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are infinitely many primes of the form 4m+3 (construct N_k = 2·3·5·...·p_k - 1 to force a new 4m+3 prime factor). A corollary of the two-squares theorem gives infinitely many primes 4m+1 by constructing numbers congruent 1 (mod 4) with only large prime factors and arguing via representability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are constructive existence arguments; note the reference to Dirichlet's theorem for general a m + b sequences and the remark about Chebyshev's bias describing distribution irregularities between residue classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact list (proof building blocks) for sum-of-two-squares theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Five explicit facts used in the main theorem: (1) base representables; (2) closure under multiplication with explicit formula; (3) closure under multiplying by a square; (4) primes p≡3 (mod4) dividing x^2+y^2 divide x and y; (5) consequently p^2 divides n and n/p^2 representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modular and multiplicative facts should be memorized as toolkit for composition/decomposition arguments when establishing representability or proving impossibility by local considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (Wedderburn): Every finite division ring is a field
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is a finite division ring (i.e., ring with 1 where every nonzero element has multiplicative inverse) then R is commutative; in other words, every finite division ring is a field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy uses (a) centralizers C_s and the center Z (a finite field of size q), giving vector-space dimensions and |R|=q^n; (b) action by conjugation partitions R* into conjugacy classes A_i with sizes dividing q^n - 1, producing a class formula |R*| = |Z*| + Σ |A_k|; (c) number-theoretic divisibility consequences (if q^{n_k}-1 | q^n -1 ⇒ n_k | n); (d) cyclotomic polynomial Φ_n(x) has integer coefficients with constant ±1 so Φ_n(q) is an integer > q-1, contradiction with divisibility by q-1. Key lemmas: properties of roots of unity and cyclotomic polynomials; use of complex roots to estimate sizes. Guidance includes references to Wedderburn, Dickson, Witt proofs and explanation of the 'coup de grâce' step using evaluation at q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class formula and divisibility lemma in finite division ring argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugacy classes under x ↦ x^{-1} s x partition R*; non-central classes have size |A| = (q^{n} - 1)/(q^{n_s} - 1) times something; from q^{n_k} - 1 | q^n - 1 one deduces n_k | n (write n = a n_k + r and use relative primality). Hence n_k ≤ n and n_k | n for all k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This number-theoretic divisibility observation is used to reach contradiction after combining with cyclotomic polynomial size estimates. Keep track of vector-space dimensions over the center and sizes of multiplicative groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Niven's method and lemma for irrationality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct polynomials f(x) with integer coefficients and controlled size (0<f(x)<1 for 0<x<1) whose derivatives at 0 and 1 are integers; then build linear combinations F(x) of derivatives and use integrals/estimates to reach contradictions assuming rationality of e^r or related constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma: choose f(x)=x^n(1-x)^n / n! times integer coefficients so that f^(k)(0) and f^(k)(1) are integers and 0<f(x)<1 on (0,1). Use this to form F with differential identity d/dx[e^{s x} F(x)] = s^{2n+1} e^{s x} f(x) to get integer integrals N that are squeezed to non-integers by size estimates, forcing contradictions. This is the template for Theorem 1 (e^r irrational) and variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 1: e^r irrational for rational r≠0
rubrics_metrics.description: For every rational r ≠ 0, e^r is irrational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to positive integer s, assume e^s = a/b rational, choose n large so n! > a s^{2n+1}, construct F(x) as combination of integer-derivative polynomial f(x) and derivatives scaled by s powers; integrate derivative identity to obtain integer N satisfying 0<N<1 contradiction. Use explicit growth estimates n! > e^{(something)} to pick n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 2: π^2 is irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: π^2 is irrational (proved by a variant of Niven/Hermite method).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume π^2 rational and form an appropriate polynomial combination F(x) (using sine/cosine in integration identity) so that an integral N = ∫ f(x) sin(π x) dx is integer and 0<N<1 for large n, contradiction. Legendre-type lemma on 2-adic valuation of n! (max power of 2 in n!) is used with n chosen as a power of two to control denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3: irrationality of certain arccos multiples (A(n))
rubrics_metrics.description: For every odd integer n ≥ 3 the number A(n) := n · arccos(½) (?) is irrational. (Text states A(n):= - arccos(5) with OCR artifacts; the theorem asserts certain multiples of arccos of rational values are irrational for odd n.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses cosine addition theorem to produce integer sequences A_k with recursion A_{k+1} = 2 A_k - n A_{k-1}; show A_k are integers not divisible by n, and deduce contradiction if A(n) rational. Intended application: Hilbert's third problem for n=3 and n=9. (Note: consult original text for exact arccos argument and constants because OCR in chunk may distort numerics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's series identity ζ(2) = π^2/6 and multiple proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Basel problem: Σ_{n≥1} 1/n^2 = π^2 / 6. Several elegant proofs are presented including evaluating a double integral in two ways (series expansion then change of variables) and Beukers–Calabi–Kolk coordinate-transform proof splitting even/odd terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First method: express integral I = ∫∫ 1/(1-xy) dx dy over [0,1]^2, expand geometric series and integrate termwise to get Σ 1/n^2; then change variables (u=(x+y)/2?, or u=(x+y)/√2 etc. per text) to evaluate integral as π^2/6. Beukers method: split series into even/odd parts and use nontrivial coordinate transform to compute a related integral J. Guidance includes substitution formula/Jacobian comment and geometric interpretation (rotate and scale square).
